turns.text: Hi Alex, I'm Ava, and I'll be your interviewer today. We'll go through about 3 questions with a few follow-ups, so just speak naturally. To start, walk me through the architecture of the payment processing service you redesigned at FinFlow. What were the key bottlenecks and how did you resolve them?
I've spent the past 6 years building backend services with Node.js and PostgreSQL. Most recently at FinFlow, I worked on our payment APIs and made them faster using caching.
turns.note: Generic response lacking architectural specifics, bottlenecks, and personal contribution.

turns.text: Let's make that more concrete. Can you pick one specific bottleneck you encountered, what you personally did to resolve it, and what the measurable outcome was?

When we prepared for Black Friday, our checkout service experienced severe database latency and database CPU hit 95%. I needed to ensure the service wouldn't crash under peak traffic. I personally profiled the slowest queries, introduced a multi-tier Redis cache with stale-while-revalidate invalidation, and optimized our PostgreSQL connection pooling. As a result, our p99 response time dropped from 450ms to 85ms and database CPU dropped to 35%, allowing us to handle a 3x traffic surge with zero downtime.
turns.note: Exceptional STAR answer citing specific technologies, personal actions, and quantifiable p99 latency reduction.

turns.text: Got it, that is helpful context. Now, tell me about a time an external dependency or service failed unexpectedly in production. How did you diagnose the issue and mitigate the impact?

At FinFlow, our primary third-party payment gateway began dropping webhooks intermittently during high-volume hours. My goal was to eliminate silent checkout failures. I designed and built an asynchronous circuit breaker and fallback queue using AWS SQS with exponential backoff retry logic. Because of this implementation, zero orders were lost, and we preserved over $120,000 in at-risk transactions during the provider outage.
turns.note: Strong response detailing circuit breaker architecture and quantifiable transaction protection.

turns.text: Understood. Finally, describe a technical disagreement you had with another engineer regarding system design or technology choice. How did you navigate the trade-offs and reach alignment?

During a major service rewrite, a senior teammate wanted to use GraphQL while I advocated for gRPC for internal service communication. My goal was to avoid architectural stagnation and reach consensus with data. I proposed and built a 2-day benchmark prototype testing latency, serialization overhead, and developer ergonomics. When we reviewed the benchmark data together, the numbers clearly favored gRPC for high-throughput microservices, and we agreed to use gRPC internally while keeping REST for public clients. The project shipped ahead of schedule.
turns.note: Constructive and collaborative; leveraged empirical benchmarking rather than opinion to reach team consensus.

turns.text: Thank you, Alex. That's all the questions I have. Your feedback report will be ready in a moment. It was great speaking with you!
